territorial_scope.description: A California state statute that applies to developers of covered models and operators of computing clusters within the state's legal framework, with no explicit extraterritorial reach stated.

evidence.quote: Chapter 22.6 (commencing with Section 22602) is added to Division 8 of the Business and Professions Code

summary.short: Adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 22.6 requiring developers of covered AI models to maintain safety and security protocols, assess critical-harm risk, undergo annual audits and report incidents to the Attorney General; also imposes customer checks on compute clusters. Several duties apply from January 1, 2026.
summary.long: Adds Business and Professions Code Chapter 22.6 for developers of 'covered models': models trained with over 10^26 operations costing over $100 million (fine-tuning: 3×10^25 operations and $10 million), with later thresholds set by a state agency from 2027. Before training, developers must implement cybersecurity protections, a full-shutdown capability and a written safety and security protocol. Before use or release, they must assess whether the model can cause a 'critical harm' (such as mass-casualty CBRN weapons or large cyberattacks on critical infrastructure), safeguard against it, and not release it if the risk is unreasonable. Developers publish redacted protocols, file annual compliance statements with the Attorney General, report safety incidents within 72 hours, and obtain annual independent audits from 2026. Computing-cluster operators must verify customers and keep records. The Attorney General may sue for civil penalties (10% of training compute cost for a first violation, 30% thereafter, for violations causing harm or imminent risk), injunctions and damages; whistleblower protections apply. A nine-member Board of Frontier Models is created, and a CalCompute public cloud framework is to be developed, subject to appropriation.

relations.note: The covered-model duties in Section 22603 do not apply where they would strictly conflict with a contract with a federal government entity. They still apply to uses not covered by such a contract.

evidence.quote: This section shall not apply to products or services to the extent that the requirements would strictly conflict with the terms of a contract with a federal government entity

relations.target_text: guidance of the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute and the National Institute of Standards and Technology
relations.note: Developers must consider this guidance (22603(i), 22604(b)). Regulations and guidance under Gov. Code 11547.6(e)(2) and (f)(2) must be consistent with it.

evidence.quote: Any regulations issued pursuant to paragraph (1) shall, at a minimum, be consistent with guidance issued by the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute and the National Institute of Standards and Technology.

notes: The registry marks the bill as vetoed, but the supplied document is bill text without legislative history, so the veto is not shown in the document. Covered-model thresholds change on 1 January 2027: before that date, fixed values apply (22602(e)(1)(A)); after it, thresholds are set by Government Operations Agency regulation (22602(e)(1)(B)), with the pre-2027 values as fallback if no regulation is adopted (22602(e)(1)(B)(ii)). Auditor duties start 1 January 2026 (22603(e)(1)), but the binding audit rules are due by 1 January 2027 (Gov. Code 11547.6(e)(1)). Section 8 contains a public-access finding under Cal. Const. art. I, sec. 3.

thresholds.variable_text: damage from cyberattacks on critical infrastructure in critical harm definition
thresholds.value_text: at least five hundred million dollars ($500,000,000) of damage
thresholds.measurement: Damage resulting from cyberattacks on critical infrastructure by a model
thresholds.consequence: Damage at this level, alternatively to mass casualties, is a critical harm under the chapter.
thresholds.conditions: Alternative to mass casualties; requires a model conducting or providing precise instructions for a cyberattack on critical infrastructure.

evidence.quote: Mass casualties or at least five hundred million dollars ($500,000,000) of damage resulting from cyberattacks on critical infrastructure

thresholds.variable_text: damage from autonomous AI model conduct in critical harm definition

thresholds.measurement: Damage resulting from an AI model engaging in conduct with limited human oversight
thresholds.consequence: Damage at this level, alternatively to mass casualties, is a critical harm under the chapter.
thresholds.conditions: Alternative to mass casualties; requires conduct with limited human oversight that results in death, great bodily injury, property damage or property loss and would be a crime if committed by a human.
